g.welcome.h1: Ask the bonsai masters of Japan, in your own words.
g.ask.hint: Write the way you talk. Claude carries your meaning into {A} bonsai terms.
g.q: I wired this juniper a few months ago. Now the wire near the top looks tight on the branch. When should I take it off, and how? I'm also worried the branch will spring back.
g.ans.h: Take the top wire off now. Where it bites, cut it off one turn at a time.
g.ans.p1: From your photo, the wire near the top looks like it is getting tight. The branch has most likely set by now, so take the wire off before the mark gets deeper. This step is called [[hazushi:wire removal]].
g.ans.p2: Where the wire has bitten in, don't unwind it. Unwinding can tear the bark and twist the branch. Snip it with wire cutters, one turn at a time.
g.ans.p3: On a juniper, a faint mark usually fades as the branch thickens.
g.ans.p4: Don't [[kake:rewire]] it right away. If the branch springs back, wait until the tree is growing strongly again, then wire it in the opposite direction so the new wire doesn't sit in the old marks.
g.ans.tnote: Translated for meaning by Claude. Japanese bonsai terms are kept and explained.
g.ans.mini: Your question · Juniper, wired a few months ago
g.gloss.hazushi.p: Taking training wire off once the branch has set, before it scars the bark. Where the wire has bitten in, it is cut off turn by turn instead of unwound.
g.gloss.kake.p: Coiling copper or aluminium wire around a branch to guide where it grows. When a branch is rewired, the new wire is wound the opposite way so it does not sit in the old marks.
g.gloss.src: Japanese bonsai term · explained by Claude

g.qa2.q: When should I cut the new shoots on my black pine?
g.qa2.a: In early summer, on a healthy tree. This is called [[mekiri:mekiri]].
g.qa3.q: My maple's leaf edges turn brown in summer. Why?
g.qa3.a: Usually strong afternoon sun or dry wind. Give it shade after midday.
g.qa4.q: When is the right time to repot my azalea?
g.qa4.a: Right after it flowers, before the new roots start to run.
g.qa5.q: My ume didn't flower this year.
g.qa5.a: Ume sets next year's buds in summer. Hard pruning after midsummer cuts them off.

g.qa.deskQ: Is it too late to cut the new shoots on my black pine in August?
g.qa.deskA: From the masters' answers: cut the new shoots in early summer, on a healthy tree. This is [[mekiri:mekiri]]. August is late, and the new buds may not harden before winter. Wait until next summer.

g.learn.lead: Bonsai terms stay in Japanese, with a meaning you can read. Tap one to open it.
g.gloss.mekiri.p: Cutting off this year's new shoots on black pine in early summer. The tree grows a second, smaller set, so its branches stay short and fine.
g.gloss.jin.p: A dead branch stripped of bark and kept on purpose. The white wood shows what the tree has lived through.
g.gloss.nebari.p: Roots that spread out from the base of the trunk, above the soil. Strong surface roots make a tree look settled and old.
g.gloss.uekae.p: Taking the tree out of its pot every few years, trimming the roots and changing the soil. It keeps the roots young.
g.gloss.metsumi.p: Pinching off soft new growth with the fingers to keep the tree compact and balanced.
g.gloss.tachiagari.p: The first part of the trunk, from the soil up to the first branch. Masters look here first when they judge a tree.

g.art1.t: Why the words stay in Japanese
g.art1.p:
Bonsai has its own Japanese vocabulary, and a word-for-word translation often points the wrong way. Harigane-hazushi literally means "wire removal", but what matters is the timing and the method: take the wire off once the branch has set, and cut it off where it bites instead of unwinding it.

So BONSAIGO keeps the Japanese term and puts a plain meaning next to it. Tap any term in an answer to see what it means and why masters do it. Over time, the same words let growers in many countries talk about the same tree.
g.art2.t: Your first year: water, light, soil
g.art2.p:
Most trees in a small pot dry out faster than you expect. Water when the surface of the soil starts to dry, and water until it runs out of the bottom of the pot.

Most outdoor bonsai, such as pines and junipers, want sun and fresh air. Keep them outside, and protect them from the strongest midday heat in summer.

Bonsai soil drains quickly on purpose. That is why roots get air and do not rot. If water sits on top for a long time, it may be time to repot.
g.art3.t: Reading a tree like a master
g.art3.p:
When masters look at a tree, they often start at the bottom. Nebari is how the roots spread out from the base of the trunk. Strong, even surface roots make a tree look settled and old.

Next is tachiagari, the lower trunk up to the first branch. Its movement sets the character of the whole tree.

Only then do they look at the branches. Before you ask a question, try taking one photo from the front at pot height. It helps the master read your tree.
